title: Kaveh the Blacksmith
text:
In the Shahnameh, the tyrant Zahhak ruled Iran with two serpents growing from his shoulders. Each day the serpents had to be fed the brains of two young men, and the kingdom paid in sons. Haunted by a dream that a young man named Fereydun would overthrow him, Zahhak decided to protect his name. He had a document drawn up declaring him a just and generous king, and he made the nobles sign it. Out of fear, they all did.

At that moment a blacksmith named Kaveh burst into the court, crying out for justice. He had had eighteen sons, and seventeen had already been taken for the serpents. Now the last one had been seized. Zahhak, wanting to look merciful, returned the boy and asked Kaveh to add his name to the declaration.

Kaveh read it, turned on the nobles and called them shameless for signing, then tore the document to pieces and walked out. In the market he raised his leather blacksmith's apron on the point of a spear and called on the people to follow him. Crowds gathered behind the apron, and Kaveh led them to Fereydun.

Fereydun covered the apron with jewels and made it his royal banner. With that army he defeated Zahhak and chained him inside Mount Damavand.
lesson: Unjust power often depends on respectable people signing what they know is false. Refusing to lend your name to a lie can be the act that gives others the courage to stand up.
source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, the reign of Zahhak
